title: How do you know when an automated crypto trading bot has stopped working?
author: alittlebitnostalgic
selftext:
I keep seeing the same pattern with almost every agent I test.  
  
The backtest looks like its sorta working. Then when you start paper trading, it turns out to be decent-ish.  
  
But when it goes live, the performance starts dropping and it slowly bleeds. Maybe mostly because of fees, slippage, or even market conditions changing realtime.  
  
I'm starting to think the bigger problem is figuring out when a bot should get access to real money, and knowing when to pull the plug once it's running  
  
My rough process right now is to backtest with harsh fees, paper trade for at least 2 weeks, start live with tiny size, and pause it if the live drawdown exceeds the worst drawdown from backtesting.  
  
It's what happens after going live that I struggle with. I either leave it running for too long or keep tweaking things until I break the strategy myself.  
  
How are you guys handling ai bots/agents like this? And how often do you review a bot that's already running?

comments.author: AoideusWasBanned
comments.body: Paper fills never matched my backtest assumptions either. I started comparing each paper trade to what the backtest would do on the same candles. When they drift apart it's usually fees or slippage, not the strategy.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: you were asking about the walk-away number on your agents thread last week, and this is where it pays. the check I'd add: log the price each live trade expected and the price it got. if that gap per trade is bigger than the cost you backtested with, it's fees and slippage, not the market changing. what cost per side did the backtest assume?

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Your process is already solid, and pausing when live drawdown passes the backtest worst case is a good line. For the part after going live, I'd decide the review rules in advance so you're not judging on gut feel. Compare live results to the backtest trade by trade, looking at fees and slippage per trade, since that's usually where the bleed starts. Review on a fixed schedule or after a set number of trades, and don't change anything between reviews. That stops the constant tweaking. For the testing side, Cymetica's Backtest Labs lets you add fees and holds out the last part of the history.
